title: Kdrama Data
text:
I am a big fan of Korean dramas, in this project I want to explore the data put togethere by apoorvareddy612 Kdramas_Analysis to answer the follwing questions: - What are the most common genre among these series - Which actor is involved in the most dramas
In this project, I will use:

at least 3 different str_*() functions
at least 1 fct_*() function
at least 3 regular expressions
at least 1 lookaround
at least 2 illustrative, well-labeled plots or tables
a description of what insights can be gained from your plots and tables



Code
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
kdrama <- read.csv(
"https://raw.githubusercontent.com/apoorvareddy612/Kdramas_Analysis/main/kdrama.csv")


These are the main genres (genre1) of the kdramas listed in the data.


Code
#splitting up the genre
kdrama <- kdrama |> 
  mutate(
    #breaking down the genres 
    genre1 = str_extract(Genre, "\\w+"),
    genre2 = str_extract(Genre, "(?<=,)[^,]+"),
    genre_remainings = str_extract(Genre, "(?:[^,]*,){2}[^,]+$"),
    genre2 = str_trim(genre2)) #to remove whitespaces

#see what are the main genres
kdrama |> 
  pull(genre1) |> 
  unique()


 [1] "Fantasy"    "Romance"    "Workplace"  "Action"     "Legal"     
 [6] "Drama"      "Sports"     "Comedy"     "Crime"      "Family"    
[11] "Science"    "Horror"     "Dark"       "Coming"     "Mystery"   
[16] "Medical"    "Historical" "Thriller"   "Suspense"   "Musical"   
[21] "Slice"      "Revenge"    "Time"      


Code
#combining the less frequent genres
kdrama <- kdrama |> 
  mutate(
    genre_group = fct_collapse(
      as.factor(genre1),
    `Action & Suspense` = c("Action", "Thriller", "Suspense", 
    "Mystery", "Crime", "Revenge", "Dark", "Horror"),
    `Comedy & Family` = c("Comedy", "Family", "Coming", "Slice"),
    Professional = c("Workplace", "Legal", "Medical", "Science"),
    `Historical & Time` = c("Historical", "Time"),
    Other = c("Sports", "Musical")))

#bar graph showing the count of genres
ggplot(kdrama, aes(x = fct_infreq(genre_group)))+
  geom_bar()+
  labs(
    title = "Number of K-dramas by genre group",
    x = "Genre",
    y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 45,
      hjust = 1))









The bar graph above shows the count of each genre (group). Out of the 23 main genres, only “Romance”, “Fantacy”, and “Drama” were not grouped. While there are many different genres in kdrama, “Romance” remains the main theme across 270 dramas.


Code
#creating new dataframe for actors
actor_data <- kdrama |>
  select(Drama.Name, Actors, Rating.Out.of.10.) |>
  #split up the Actors string into rows, each row is an actor in a kdrama
  separate_longer_delim(Actors, delim = ",") |>  
  mutate(Actors = str_trim(Actors)) #trim whitespace


head(actor_data)


              Drama.Name         Actors Rating.Out.of.10.
1 Legend of the Blue Sea    Jun Ji-hyun               8.1
2 Legend of the Blue Sea     Lee Min-ho               8.1
3              The Heirs     Lee Min-ho               7.5
4              The Heirs  Park Shin-hye               7.5
5              The Heirs    Kim Woo-bin               7.5
6              The Heirs Park Hyung-sik               7.5


Code
#actors performance statistics
actor_summary <- actor_data |> 
  group_by(Actors) |> 
  summarize(
    drama_count = n_distinct(Drama.Name), #count the number of distinct dramas one participated in
    avg_rating = mean(Rating.Out.of.10., na.rm = TRUE),
    .group = "drop") #count the average rating among their dramas 

head(actor_summary)


# A tibble: 6 × 4
  Actors       drama_count avg_rating .group
  <chr>              <int>      <dbl> <chr> 
1 Ahn Bo-hyun            5       7.88 drop  
2 Ahn Da-eun             1       6.8  drop  
3 Ahn Do-gyu             1       6.8  drop  
4 Ahn Dong-goo           1       7.7  drop  
5 Ahn Eun-jin            2       8.65 drop  
6 Ahn Hyo-seop           5       7.58 drop  


Code
#scatterplot showing the top 15 actors with the highest average rating dramas
actor_summary |>
  filter(drama_count >= 3) |>
  slice_max(avg_rating, n = 15) |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = avg_rating,
    y = reorder(Actors, avg_rating)
  )) +
  geom_point(
    size = 3,
    shape = "triangle"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Average drama rating",
    y = "Actor",
    title = "Actors in the highest-rated K-dramas",
    subtitle = "Limited to actors with at least 3 drama appearances"
  )









The graph above illustrates the top 15 actors who appeared in at least 3 dramas that has the highest average rating (not their personal performance but their acting could be the reason for the high rating). Dramas that Kim Tae-Ri took part in have the highest average rating of all; as someone who is a huge fan of her acting, I am more than happy to observe this result.

title: Permutation Test
text:
Credit:
Laksika Tharmalingam created this dataset and is available on Kaggle, where I downloaded the CSV file.
Dataset Overview:
The Sleep Health and Lifestyle Dataset comprises 374 rows and 13 columns, covering a wide range of variables related to sleep and daily habits. It includes details such as gender, age, occupation, sleep duration, quality of sleep, physical activity level, stress levels, BMI category, blood pressure, heart rate, daily steps, and the presence or absence of sleep disorder. Each row represents a person.
In this permutation test, I will use columns:

Stress Level (scale: 1-10): A subjective rating of the stress level experienced by the person, ranging from 1 to 10.
Physical Activity Level (minutes/day): The number of minutes the person engages in physical activity daily.

Question of interest:
This semester, I started to work out more frequently and I found myself having a better mood and more energy whenever I hit the gym. Therefore, I want to explore whether people who do more physical activity have lower stress levels. In this test, we will first split up the dataset into high- or low-physical-activity groups. Then we will compare the average stress level of the two groups and use a permutation test to ask whether a difference that large could plausibly arise by chance if physical activity and stress were unrelated. We do this by repeatedly shuffling the stress scores across people, recording the difference in group averages each time, and checking where our observed difference falls in that distribution of shuffled differences.
The null hypothesis is that the stress level will be the same regardless of their daily physical activity. The alternative hypothesis is that more exercise leads to lower stress level.


Code
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyverse)
health <- read_csv("Sleep_health_and_lifestyle_dataset.csv")




Code
health |> 
    summarize(avg_exercise = mean(`Physical Activity Level`, na.rm = TRUE), med_exercise = median(`Physical Activity Level`))


# A tibble: 1 × 2
  avg_exercise med_exercise
         <dbl>        <dbl>
1         59.2           60


Based on the median and average minutes of physical activity, we will use 60 as a cutoff:

Equal or more than 60 minutes will be the “more” group.
Less than 60 minutes will be the “less” group.



Code
#adding a column that indicates the group
health <- health |> 
    select(`Physical Activity Level`, `Stress Level`) |> 
    mutate(
        Exercise = if_else(`Physical Activity Level` >= 60, "more", "less")
    )

#calculate and show the observed statistics between 2 groups
health |> 
    group_by(Exercise) |> 
    summarize(
        num_people = n(),
        avg_stress = mean(`Stress Level`),
        avg_exercise_time = mean(`Physical Activity Level`),
        med_exercise_time = median(`Physical Activity Level`) 
    )


# A tibble: 2 × 5
  Exercise num_people avg_stress avg_exercise_time med_exercise_time
  <chr>         <int>      <dbl>             <dbl>             <dbl>
1 less            161       5.80              38.5                42
2 more            213       5.08              74.8                75


This boxplot visualized the self-rated stress level by exercise groups. The group that exercise less (than 60 minutes) had a higher stress level of median = 7, while those exercise more (than 60 minutes) reported a lower stress level (median = 5).


Code
health |> 
    ggplot(aes(x = Exercise, y = `Stress Level`))+
    geom_boxplot()+
    labs(x = "Exercise groups",
    y = "Self-rated Stress Level (1-10)",
    title = "Stress level by exercise group")









To simulate what we’d see if exercise has no relationship with stress, we first wrote a function, perm_health(), that performs one round of the simulation. If the null hypothesis is true, which group a person belongs to doesn’t matter, so randomly reassigning stress scores across people should produce differences in group averages that arise purely by chance.
In each round, the function (1) shuffles all the stress levels among the people in the data, (2) calculates the average stress level for the “more” and “less” exercise groups using both the original and the shuffled scores, and (3) returns the difference between those averages (more minus less) for both. (4) The argument rep isn’t used in the calculation. It labels which shuffle each result comes from.


Code
#create a function that shuffles the stress level among all data and calculated the averages
perm_health <- function(rep, health){
    health |> 
        mutate(stress_perm = sample(`Stress Level`, replace = FALSE)) |> #(1)
        group_by(Exercise) |> 
        summarize( #(2)
            observe_avg = mean(`Stress Level`), #original score
            perm_avg = mean(stress_perm) #shuffled score
        ) |> 
        summarize( #(3)
            observe_avg_diff = diff(observe_avg),
            perm_avg_diff = diff(perm_avg),
            rep = rep #(4)
        )
}


One shuffle isn’t enough to tell us what chance looks like, so we use map() to run the function 1000 times, once for each number from 1 to 1000, passing the same dataset each time. list_rbind() stacks the 1000 results into one data frame, and set.seed() makes the shuffles reproducible, so the results don’t change each time the document is rendered.


Code
#obtain the data with 1000-times shuffling
set.seed(1000) #fix the results of this shuffle
perm_stats <- map(c(1:1000), perm_health, health) |> 
    list_rbind()


perm_stats |> 
    ggplot(aes(x = perm_avg_diff))+
    geom_histogram(binwidth = .07)+
    geom_vline(aes(xintercept = observe_avg_diff, color = "Observed average difference \n-0.72"))+
    scale_color_manual(values = c("Observed average difference \n-0.72" = "red"))+
    labs(
        title = "Null sampling distribution (Average)",
        subtitle = "Bindwith = .07",
        x = "Permuted difference in average stress (more minus less)",
        y = "Number of shuffles"
    )









The histogram shows the 1000 permuted differences, which is the null distribution: the differences in average stress we’d expect from chance alone. The red line marks the difference actually observed in the data (-0.72), which is inconsistent with the null distribution.
The p-value is the probability of seeing a difference in average stress at least as extreme as ours, if exercise and stress are unrelated. Out of 1000 shuffles, none produced a difference as low as the observed -0.72, so the p-value is < 0.001.


Code
perm_stats |>
  summarize(
    p_val_ave = mean(observe_avg_diff > perm_avg_diff))


# A tibble: 1 × 1
  p_val_ave
      <dbl>
1         0


Because this is well below the threshold (p < 0.05), we reject the null hypothesis. The data provide strong evidence that people in the more-exercise group have lower average stress than those in the less-exercise group, which is consistent with our alternative hypothesis. This matches the histogram above, where the observed difference falls far outside the range of differences produced by chance.
One thing to keep in mind is that, physical activity is just one of the factors that could contribute to stress level specifically in this dataset. There could be other factors such as sleep duration, nutrition, occupation, etc., affect stress levels.

title: Ethical dilemma: AI recruitment and gender discrimination at Amazon
text:
In this project, we will explore an ethical dilemma in the data science context and answer a few questions inspired by the following two quotes from Data Feminism. The first asks about who and the second asks about why.
“[Examine] how power operates in the world today. This consists of asking who questions about data science: Who does the work (and who is pushed out)? Who benefits (and who is neglected or harmed)? Whose priorities get turned into products (and whose are overlooked)?”
“How did we get to the point where data science is used almost exclusively in the service of profit (for a few), surveillance (of the minoritized), and efficiency (amidst scarcity)?.”
The ethical dilemma I want to explore is whether historical applicant data should be used to train recruitment algorithms when that data reflects existing inequalities. In 2018, Reuters reported that Amazon developed an experimental recruitment tool trained on resumes submitted over a ten-year period. Because resumes predominantly came from men, the algorithm learned patterns that favoured male applicants and penalized terms associated with women. Although Amazon attempted to correct these biases, it could not ensure that the algorithm would not find other ways to discriminate, and eventually abandoned the project (Dastin, 2018).
What interests me most about this case is not simply that the algorithm was biased, but how the data used to train it contributed to that bias. The resumes reflected a historically male-dominated technology industry, yet Amazon used those patterns to evaluate future applicants. This raises the question of whether data that accurately reflects the past is necessarily appropriate for predicting the future. I am also interested in how applicants’ personal data is collected and whether they understand how it may be used beyond their individual job applications. I also examined the current Amazon privacy notice website to understand further how data could’ve been collected (Amazon, n.d.). As an international student, I find this especially concerning because I already face additional barriers in the job market, i.e. needing visa sponsorship. If an automated system were to treat sponsorship requirements or other characteristics of my background as undesirable, I could be excluded before anyone considered my actual qualifications. This case makes me question whose experiences are represented in training data, whose opportunities are overlooked, and who has the power to decide how applicants are evaluated.
1. Who was measured? Were they representative of the people to whom we want to generalize?
Amazon trained its algorithm using resumes submitted over a ten-year period. According to Reuters, most of these resumes came from men, reflecting the gender imbalance in the technology industry (Dastin, 2018). However, the algorithm was intended to evaluate future applicants, including women who were underrepresented in the industry back then. This is a great example of why having a large dataset does not necessarily mean having a more generalized or representative dataset: the dataset could be biased at the very beginning. The algorithm learned from who had applied in the past, rather than necessarily learning what makes someone qualified for a job. If women had fewer opportunities or were less represented in certain technical positions historically, the algorithm could reproduce that inequality by treating the patterns in men’s resumes as the standard for success.
2. How were the variables collected? Were they accurately recorded? Is there missing data?
I imagined the variables for the resume dataset simply be each word stripped from the resume when applicants submitted for the position. The algorithm then analyzed the words and learned the patterns. In this case, the variables are accurately recorded; however, Reuters reported that it favoured certain verbs that appeared more frequently on men’s resumes, such as “executed” and “captured,” while penalizing other terms associated with women (Dastin, 2018). Which links to the first question: a more diverse spectrum of data is missing. I do not think the words someone uses to describe their experiences necessarily reflect their actual abilities. Resume language can be influenced by cultural differences, confidence, access to career advice, how people have been socialized to describe their accomplishments, and, of course, gender. The problem is not necessarily that the data was recorded incorrectly, but that the algorithm may have interpreted the data in a way that does not accurately measure what the company actually cares about: a candidate’s ability to perform the job.
3. What is the permission and consent structure for using the data? Was it followed?
From Amazon’s Candidate Privacy Notice, it states that Amazon collects information such as resumes, demographic data, screening-question responses, work preferences, assessment results, and interview notes to manage the recruitment process. It also explains that candidate information may be retained after an unsuccessful application for purposes such as contacting applicants about future jobs, recordkeeping, and legal proceedings (Amazon, n.d.). While the notice explains the general collection and use of applicants’ personal data, it does not, in the version I reviewed, specifically explain that resumes would be used to train an experimental machine-learning recruitment model like the one described in the Reuters article. I cannot conclude from these two sources alone that Amazon violated applicants’ consent or privacy rights, especially because the privacy notice available today may not be the same as the notice applicants received when the experiment was developed. However, it raises an ethical question about whether applicants truly understand how their information might be used beyond evaluating their individual applications. Applying for a job requires sharing personal information, but that does not necessarily mean applicants expect their data to be repurposed to train algorithms that may influence future applicants’ opportunities. I think there should be greater transparency about how applicant data is used, particularly when it is being used to develop systems that could affect other people’s employment opportunities.
4. Recognize and mitigate bias in ourselves and in the data we use.
The Data Values and Principles manifesto emphasizes recognizing and mitigating bias in ourselves and in the data we use. Amazon’s case demonstrates that algorithms are not automatically objective just because they rely on mathematical calculations. The bias came partly from historical inequality in the technology industry, but also from the decision to use past resumes as a basis for predicting future candidates’ suitability. Amazon attempted to remove specific discriminatory patterns, such as penalizing the word “women’s,” but this did not guarantee that other forms of discrimination would disappear. I think developers need to consider not only whether a model performs accurately overall, but also who it performs poorly for and why. It is also important to have people with different backgrounds involved in developing and evaluating these systems, because people who are affected by potential discrimination may notice problems that developers themselves overlook. Amazon’s decision to abandon the tool then recognized that fixing a few biased variables was not enough to guarantee fairness.
Why does this matter?
Amazon’s recruitment tool illustrates how data science can reinforce existing power structures instead of challenging them. The company could benefit from faster and more efficient recruitment, but applicants could be harmed if they were ranked lower because of characteristics unrelated to their ability to do the job. For me, this issue is particularly concerning because job applicants often have very little control over how their applications are evaluated. We may not know whether AI is being used, what information it is analyzing, or why our applications are rejected. As an international student, I already face additional considerations when searching for employment, and I worry that an automated system could create another barrier that I cannot see or challenge. The problem is not simply that AI makes mistakes, but that those mistakes could be scaled across thousands of applicants while remaining invisible to the people affected. In the context of Data Feminism, this case makes me question whose priorities are being served by data science. If the primary goal is efficiency and reducing the cost of recruitment, fairness and individual circumstances may become secondary. I believe AI should support recruiters in evaluating candidates, rather than become an invisible gatekeeper that determines who gets the opportunity to be considered in the first place.
Reference:
Amazon. (n.d.). Global employment candidate privacy notice. https://www.amazon.jobs/en/privacy_page
Data Practices. (n.d.). Data values and principles. https://datapractices.org/manifesto/
Dastin, J. (2018, October 10). Amazon scraps secret AI recruiting tool that showed bias against women. Reuters. https://www.reuters.com/article/us-amazon-com-jobs-automation-insight/amazon-scraps-secret-ai-recruiting-tool-that-showed-bias-against-women/
D’Ignazio, C., & Klein, L. F. (2020). Data feminism. The MIT Press. https://data-feminism.mitpress.mit.edu/
